standard.goal: Whoever builds or changes the product, a person or an AI, makes each part without hesitating and on the same thinking as every other part, so the parts together deliver the UX and the product stays easy to read and to change.

parts.what: The title, "<Product name> architecture", and the sentence or two under it that say how the product delivers its UX, with a link to the UX.

The Principles section: one subsection for each principle, holding the rule and its reason, after a link to the principles of the architecture this one is built on, where there is one. Each subsection is headed with a short name for the principle; the rule is one sentence that every part is built by; the reason says what the rule is there for, and what goes wrong for the user or the builder without it.

The User stories section: a list under its heading, one item for each story, each naming the UX's scenarios or steps that rest on it. Each item reads "As <the user>, I want <one way they use the product at its edge, such as a command they run>. Carries <the UX's scenarios, or their steps, that rest on it>."

The figure under Components, the first subsection of the Logical view section: an SVG file beside the document drawn by hand in the notation of a C4 component diagram. It has a box for each role the user stories need and each store of data, holding its name and a tag of its type and technology, such as "[web app · React, TypeScript]" or "[database · PostgreSQL]", and no sentence; its shape saying its kind of element; each arrow what one does to another, with the data it hands on, named as in the data model, and the protocol where it matters, such as "[HTTPS/JSON]"; and a legend of the shapes and the tags. The boxes are placed so the arrows run in the order they act and cross none.
The first items of the list under Components: what a role alone is responsible for that no arrow shows.
The items of the lists under Components, Sequences, Deployment and Test that give a choice the reader would question, such as a technology or a tool, with why it was made over the other way.

The figure under Data model, the second subsection of the Logical view section: an SVG file beside the document drawn by hand in the notation of an ER diagram. It has a box for each data the roles pass or keep, holding the data's name alone, and a line between two data for each relation between them, labelled with the relation's name, its ends drawn in crow's-foot notation for its cardinality, such as one to many.

The UML sequence diagrams in Mermaid under Sequences, the third subsection of the Logical view section, one for each user story; a sequence has one layout, its order down the page, so Mermaid draws it from text. Each has a participant for the user, for each role the story reaches, named as in Components, and for each thing outside the product it reaches; and a message for each step, labelled in a few words with what one does and the data handed on, named as in the data model.

The figure under Deployment, the first subsection of the Physical view section: an SVG file beside the document drawn by hand in the notation of a C4 deployment diagram. Each outer box is an execution environment, such as a cloud service, a phone, the user's computer or CI, with its technology tag; it holds the deployment units, such as an app or a container, each with its technology tag and, by their names in Components, the roles that run in it and the data kept in it; and a box for each thing outside the product they depend on has an arrow labelled with what is used. The list under it gives how the product is started, and choices.

The tree under Directory structure, the second subsection of the Physical view section: the folders and files of the product, in a text block, as the files lie, each line that holds a role or a data naming it as in Components with its technology tag.

The table under Test, the last section: a row for each deployment unit, named as in Deployment with its technology tag; a column for each test type from narrow scope to wide, unit, integration and end-to-end; each cell a tool, a weight, such as ●●● or ●●○, and what it checks in a few words, as "<tool> · <weight> · <what it checks>"; an empty cell hatched, ▨, with a footnote that says why it is empty; and the note of the units left out because every cell of their row would be empty, with why.

The lines under the table: for each test type, including any the product adds, what it makes real, what it fakes and when it passes, and, for a result that varies from run to run, how many runs of how many must meet the expectation; each unit's weight with what a failure costs the user; and, at the start of Test before the table, a link to the project's shared test rules, with only what differs written here.

checklist.what: Having read the opening, can the builder say how the product delivers its UX, as one idea that every part carries out?
When two builders of different parts meet a case the document does not name, does a principle's reason lead both to the same decision?
For each step of the UX's scenarios, can the builder name the one way of using the product at its edge that carries it?
Starting on a role, can the builder begin without choosing for themselves what kind of thing it is and what it is made with?
For anything the user stories need decided, can the builder point to the one role that decides it?
When one builder makes the role that writes a data and another makes the role that reads it, do both join it to the other data the same way?
For each user story, can the builder follow it from the user's first request to its end, knowing at each step which role acts and what data it hands on?
Setting the product up from nothing, can the builder put each role where it runs and each data where it is kept, and start the product, without asking anyone?
Making or changing a role or a data, can the builder find the one place its files belong?
Asked whether anything in the product goes untested, can the builder answer, for each deployment unit, which types of test cover it, how heavily, and why a type is missing?
Writing a test of one type, can the builder do it without deciding for themselves what to make real, what to fake and when it passes?
When the builder doubts a choice the document makes, can they tell what would be lost by taking the other way?

checklist.about: principles, components, responsibilities, sequences, deployment, directory, test-table, test-rules
checklist.what: Following a principle while building a part, does the builder find every figure, list and table asking the same of that part, so they never have to choose which to follow?
Of any user story, role or data, can the builder tell which step of the UX needs it?
When the builder changes how a role works inside, while the UX and the principles stay, does every line of the document still hold?

methods.question: Q3
methods.thinking: A user story is one way the user meets the product at its edge, and the stories together carry every step the UX shows.
steps: Walk each scenario of the UX step by step, and mark each step where the user, a person or an AI, meets the product.
Group the marked steps by the way they reach the product, such as one command or one call.
Write one story for each way: "As <the user>, I want <the way>. Carries <the scenarios or steps>."
Check that every marked step is carried by one story, and add a story for a step that none carries.
grounds: Hruschka and Starke, "3. Context and Scope", arc42 documentation, docs.arc42.org, no date: "System scope and context - as the name suggests - delimits your system (i.e. your scope) from all its communication partners (neighboring systems and users, i.e. the context of your system)."

Mountain Goat Software, "User Stories: What They Are, How to Write Them, and Examples", mountaingoatsoftware.com, 2026: "A common template is: As a [type of user], I [need/want/am required] to [do something], so that [reason or benefit]."

Kruchten, "Architectural Blueprints—The “4+1” View Model of Software Architecture", IEEE Software, 1995: "as a driver to discover the architectural elements during the architecture design as we will describe later"

methods.question: Q1
methods.thinking: The opening says, in one idea, how the product turns what the user brings into what the UX promises, so every part after it reads as a piece of that idea.
steps: From the UX and the user stories, name what the user brings to the product and what they get back.
Name the few main things the product does between the two.
Write them as a sentence or two, with the product as the subject, and none of a part's inner workings.
Link the UX instead of repeating it.
Once the rest is written, check that each part carries out a piece of the idea; where one does not, change the idea or the part.
grounds: matklad, "ARCHITECTURE.md", matklad.github.io, 2021: "Start with a bird’s eye overview of the problem being solved."

rust-analyzer team, "Architecture", rust-analyzer repository, no date: "On the highest level, rust-analyzer is a thing which accepts input source code from the client and produces a structured semantic model of the code."
Fowler, "Architecture Decision Record", martinfowler.com, 2026: "The key is to put the most important material at the start, and push details to later in the record."
Hruschka and Starke, "1. Introduction and Goals", arc42 documentation, docs.arc42.org, no date: "If requirements documents exist this overview should refer to these documents."

Hruschka and Starke, "4. Solution Strategy", arc42 documentation, docs.arc42.org, no date: "These decisions form the cornerstones for your architecture. They are the basis for many other detailed decisions or implementation rules."

methods.question: Q5
methods.thinking: Roles are cut so that each decision the stories need, above all one likely to change, is made in one role alone.
steps: Walk each user story, and list what must be decided along it, first the decisions that are hard to make or likely to change.
Give each decision one role, and let that role keep it from the others.
Draw an arrow for each thing one role asks of another, labelled with what it does and the data it hands on, not with a word such as "uses".
Under the figure, write what each role alone decides that no arrow shows.
Ask of each decision which role makes it; where two roles or none answer, move the decision or split the role.
grounds: Parnas, "On the Criteria to be Used in Decomposing Systems into Modules", Carnegie-Mellon University technical report, 1971: "We propose instead that one begins with a list of difficult design decisions or design decisions which are likely to change. Each module is then designed to hide such a decision from the others."
Brown, "Component", C4 model, c4model.com, no date: "in the C4 model, a component is a grouping of related functionality encapsulated behind a well-defined interface."

Brown, "Notation", C4 model, c4model.com, no date: "Every line should be labelled, the label being consistent with the direction and intent of the relationship (e.g. dependency or data flow). Try to be as specific as possible with the label, ideally avoiding single words like, “Uses”."
Brown, "Software architecture diagram review checklist", C4 model, c4model.com, no date: "Do you understand what every element does?"

methods.question: Q4
methods.thinking: Each role's box says what kind of thing it is and what it is made with, so the builder starts on it with nothing left to choose.
steps: For each role and each store of data, choose its type, such as a service or a module, and its technology.
Write them as a tag in its box, after its name.
Give each box the shape of its kind of element, and add a legend of the shapes and the tags.
Check that every role of one kind has the same type and technology, or that a choice under the figure says why not.
Read the figure without the text around it, and add to the legend or the tags whatever the reader would still have to ask.
grounds: Brown, "Notation", C4 model, c4model.com, no date: "The type of every element should be explicitly specified (e.g. Person, Software System, Container or Component)."
Brown, "Notation", C4 model, c4model.com, no date: "Every container and component should have a technology explicitly specified."
Brown, "Notation", C4 model, c4model.com, no date: "Any notation used should be as self-describing as possible, but all diagrams should have a key/legend to make the notation explicit."
Brown, "Notation", C4 model, c4model.com, no date: "A good way to think about this is to ask yourself whether each diagram can stand alone, and be (mostly) understood without a narrative."

methods.question: Q6
methods.thinking: Each data the roles pass or keep is drawn once, with each relation to another data named and how many of each it joins.
steps: From the arrows of Components and the user stories, list each data a role passes or keeps.
Draw a box for each, holding its name alone, and leave its fields to where the data is built.
For each pair of data that refer to one another, draw a line labelled with what the relation means.
Mark both ends of the line with how many of each it joins, in crow's-foot notation.
For each line, ask whether the role that writes it and the role that reads it would keep it the same way; where they would not, name the relation more exactly.
grounds: Mermaid, "Entity Relationship Diagrams", mermaid.js.org, no date: "Relationships between entities are represented by lines with end markers representing cardinality."
Mermaid, "Entity Relationship Diagrams", mermaid.js.org, no date: "Cardinality is a property that describes how many elements of another entity can be related to the entity in question."
Ubl, "Design Docs at Google", industrialempathy.com, 2020: "Similar to the advice on APIs, and for the same reasons, copy-pasting complete schema definitions should be avoided."

methods.question: Q7
methods.thinking: Each story is traced through the roles in order, so every step of it has a role that takes it and data that it hands on.
steps: For each user story, start a Mermaid sequence diagram with the user, each role the story reaches, named as in Components, and each thing outside the product it reaches.
Write the user's first request as the first message.
Write each next step as one message from the role that takes it to the one it acts on, labelled in a few words with what it does and the data, named as in the data model.
End with the message that gives the user what the story is for.
Check that each message runs along an arrow of Components; where none does, add the arrow or give the step to another role.
grounds: Hruschka and Starke, "6. Runtime View", arc42 documentation, docs.arc42.org, no date: "The runtime view describes concrete behavior and interactions of the system’s building blocks in form of scenarios"
Hruschka and Starke, "6. Runtime View", arc42 documentation, docs.arc42.org, no date: "Always map existing building blocks to the activities within runtime scenarios!"

Brown, "Dynamic diagram", C4 model, c4model.com, no date: "A dynamic diagram can be useful when you want to show how elements in the static model collaborate at runtime to implement a user story, use case, feature, etc."
Mermaid, "Sequence diagrams", mermaid.js.org, no date: "A Sequence diagram is an interaction diagram that shows how processes operate with one another and in what order."

Kruchten, "Architectural Blueprints—The “4+1” View Model of Software Architecture", IEEE Software, 1995: "as a validation and illustration role after this architecture design is complete, both on paper and as the starting point for the tests of an architectural prototype."

methods.question: Q14
methods.thinking: Every story, role and data is there because a step of the UX needs it, so each can go once no step needs it.
steps: For each story, name the steps of the UX it carries.
For each role and each data, name the stories whose sequences reach it.
Remove a story, a role or a data that no step needs.
Remove a story for a step that happens only inside the product, and draw that step in the sequence of the story it belongs to.
grounds: Fowler, "Yagni", martinfowler.com, 2015: "The code for the presumptive feature adds some complexity to the software, this complexity makes it harder to modify and debug that software, thus increasing the cost of other features."

methods.question: Q2
methods.thinking: A principle is a rule every part meets the same way, written with what it is there for, so a builder can carry it to a case it does not name.
steps: From the roles and the sequences, list the decisions that more than one role meets, such as how a failure reaches the user.
For each, write the one rule every role follows, as one sentence a builder can check their part against.
Write as a rule also what must be absent, such as a dependency no role may have.
Under each rule, write what it is there for, and what goes wrong for the user or the builder without it.
Cut a rule that names only a means, such as a language, and rewrite one that two readers could read two ways.
Link the principles of the architecture this one is built on, and write only what this product adds or changes.
Take a case no rule names, and have two builders of different parts decide it from the reasons alone; where they differ, sharpen the reason.
grounds: Hruschka and Starke, "8. Crosscutting Concepts", arc42 documentation, docs.arc42.org, no date: "Such concepts are often related to multiple building blocks."

Hruschka and Starke, "8. Crosscutting Concepts", arc42 documentation, docs.arc42.org, no date: "It might be easier to communicate or document such cross-cutting topics at a central location, instead of repeating them in the description of the concerned building blocks, hardware elements or development processes."
matklad, "ARCHITECTURE.md", matklad.github.io, 2021: "Explicitly call-out architectural invariants."
matklad, "ARCHITECTURE.md", matklad.github.io, 2021: "Often, important invariants are expressed as an absence of something, and it’s pretty hard to divine that from reading the code."

Clements et al., "Documenting Software Architectures: Views and Beyond", 2nd edition, section P.5, informit.com, 2010: "For the most important decisions, you should record why you made them the way you did. You should also record the important or most likely alternatives you rejected and state why."

Anthropic, "Prompting best practices", Claude Platform Docs, no date: "Providing context or motivation behind your instructions, such as explaining to Claude why such behavior is important, can give Claude more information about your goals and help it deliver more targeted responses."
Anthropic, "Prompting best practices", Claude Platform Docs, no date: "Claude can generalize from the explanation."

Clements et al., "Documenting Software Architectures: Views and Beyond", 2nd edition, section P.5, informit.com, 2010: "The most dangerous kind of ambiguity is undetected ambiguity. Here, each reader will think he or she understands the document, but unwittingly each reader will come to different conclusions about what it is saying."
Clements et al., "Documenting Software Architectures: Views and Beyond", 2nd edition, section P.5, informit.com, 2010: "Each kind of information should be recorded in exactly one place."

methods.question: Q8
methods.thinking: Each role and each data is placed where it runs or is kept, so the builder knows what it can reach, and how the product starts.
steps: List each environment where a part runs or a data is kept, such as a cloud service, the user's computer or CI, with its technology.
Draw in each environment its deployment units, each with its technology tag.
Write in each unit, by their names in Components, the roles that run in it and the data kept in it.
Draw each thing outside the product that the roles depend on, with an arrow saying what is used.
Leave out any infrastructure the parts do not need.
Under the figure, write how the product is started.
Check that each role and each data of Components sits in one unit.
grounds: Brown, "Deployment diagram", C4 model, c4model.com, no date: "A deployment diagram allows you to illustrate how instances of software systems and/or containers in the static model are deployed on to the infrastructure within a given deployment environment (e.g. production, staging, development, etc)."
Brown, "Deployment diagram", C4 model, c4model.com, no date: "A deployment node represents where an instance of a software system/container is running"
Hruschka and Starke, "7. Deployment View", arc42 documentation, docs.arc42.org, no date: "Software does not run without hardware."

Hruschka and Starke, "7. Deployment View", arc42 documentation, docs.arc42.org, no date: "From a software perspective it is sufficient to capture those elements of the infrastructure that are needed to show the deployment of your building blocks."

methods.question: Q9
methods.thinking: The tree joins each role and each data to the one place where it is made, so the builder finds where to change it.
steps: Run tree on the product, or lay out the folders planned.
Keep the folders and files that hold a role or a data, and leave out what lies inside each.
On each line kept, name the role or the data it holds, as Components names it, with its technology tag.
Check that each role and each data stands on one line; where it stands on none or on two, move the files or the line.
grounds: matklad, "ARCHITECTURE.md", matklad.github.io, 2021: "The codemap should answer “where’s the thing that does X?”."
matklad, "ARCHITECTURE.md", matklad.github.io, 2021: "Do name important files, modules, and types."
matklad, "ARCHITECTURE.md", matklad.github.io, 2021: "A codemap is a map of a country, not an atlas of maps of its states."
matklad, "ARCHITECTURE.md", matklad.github.io, 2021: "Are the things you want to put near each other in the codemap adjacent when you run tree .?"

methods.question: Q10
methods.thinking: A table of each deployment unit against each scope of test shows at a glance what is tested, how heavily, and why a gap is there.
steps: Take each deployment unit from Deployment, with its tag, as a row.
Make a column for each test type, from narrow scope to wide: unit, integration and end-to-end.
In each cell, write the tool, the weight, and what it checks in a few words.
Hatch an empty cell, and give its reason in a footnote.
Leave out a unit whose every cell would be empty, and say why under the table.
Check that the wider tests are fewer, and that each user story is run end to end in some row.
grounds: Vocke, "The Practical Test Pyramid", martinfowler.com, 2018: "Write tests with different granularity"
Vocke, "The Practical Test Pyramid", martinfowler.com, 2018: "The more high-level you get the fewer tests you should have"
Bender, "Testing Overview", Software Engineering at Google, chapter 11, abseil.io, 2020: "Scope refers to the specific code paths we are verifying."

Clements et al., "Documenting Software Architectures: Views and Beyond", 2nd edition, section P.5, informit.com, 2010: "If the section is blank, the reader will wonder whether the information is coming later or whether it is indeed supposed to be blank."

methods.question: Q11
methods.thinking: Each test type is set once, with what it makes real, what it fakes and when it passes, so every test of that type means the same to every builder.
steps: Link the project's shared test rules, and write only where this product differs from them.
For each test type in the table, and each other type the product needs, write what it runs for real and what it replaces with a fake.
Write when it passes, as a bar every builder reads one way.
For a test whose result varies from run to run, write how many runs of how many must meet the expectation.
Use each type's name the same way throughout the document.
grounds: Vocke, "The Practical Test Pyramid", martinfowler.com, 2018: "A unit test typically replaces external collaborators with test doubles"
Vocke, "The Practical Test Pyramid", martinfowler.com, 2018: "For your automated tests this means you don't just need to run your own application but also the component you're integrating with."

Schwaber and Sutherland, "The Scrum Guide", scrumguides.org, 2020: "The Definition of Done is a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product."
Anthropic, "Demystifying evals for AI agents", anthropic.com/engineering, 2026: "pass^k measures the probability that all k trials succeed."

Vocke, "The Practical Test Pyramid", martinfowler.com, 2018: "Given the shortcomings of the original names it's totally okay to come up with other names for your test layers, as long as you keep it consistent within your codebase and your team's discussions."
Clements et al., "Documenting Software Architectures: Views and Beyond", 2nd edition, section P.5, informit.com, 2010: "Each kind of information should be recorded in exactly one place."

methods.question: Q13
methods.thinking: Each principle is read against every part it rules, so a builder never meets a figure, a list or a table that breaks one.
steps: For each principle, list the parts of the document it rules.
Read each of those parts against the principle, and mark each line that breaks it.
Change the part, or change the principle and its reason, until the two say the same.
Where the product departs on purpose from a principle of the architecture it is built on, say why among the choices.
grounds: Hruschka and Starke, "8. Crosscutting Concepts", arc42 documentation, docs.arc42.org, no date: "Concepts form the basis for conceptual integrity (consistency, homogeneity) of the architecture."

Kruchten, "Architectural Blueprints—The “4+1” View Model of Software Architecture", IEEE Software, 1995: "A Software Design Guidelines, which captures (among other things) the most important design decisions that must be respected to maintain the architectural integrity of the system."

Clements et al., "Documenting Software Architectures: Views and Beyond", 2nd edition, section P.5, informit.com, 2010: "Documentation that is incomplete or out of date does not reflect truth, does not obey its own rules for form and internal consistency, and is not used."

methods.question: Q12
methods.thinking: A choice a builder would question carries why it beat the other way, beside the figure that shows it, so the builder keeps it or changes it knowing what it was for.
steps: Read each figure and the table as a builder new to the product, and mark each choice they would question, such as a technology, a tool or a unit's weight.
For each, name the other way that builder would think of.
Write, in full sentences, why this way was taken over that one, and what it costs.
Put it in the list under the figure or the table that shows the choice.
For each unit's weight, write what a failure of that unit would cost the user.
grounds: Nygard, "Documenting Architecture Decisions", Cognitect blog, 2011: "Without understanding the rationale or consequences, this person has only two choices:"
Nygard, "Documenting Architecture Decisions", Cognitect blog, 2011: "Blindly accept the decision."
Nygard, "Documenting Architecture Decisions", Cognitect blog, 2011: "Blindly change it."
Ubl, "Design Docs at Google", industrialempathy.com, 2020: "The design doc is the place to write down the trade-offs you made in designing your software."

Ubl, "Design Docs at Google", industrialempathy.com, 2020: "shows very explicitly why the selected solution is the best given the project goals and how other solutions, that the reader may be wondering about, introduce trade-offs that are less desirable given the goals."
Nygard, "Documenting Architecture Decisions", Cognitect blog, 2011: "All consequences should be listed here, not just the "positive" ones."

Hruschka and Starke, "9. Architecture Decisions", arc42 documentation, docs.arc42.org, no date: "Please use your judgement to decide whether an architectural decision should be documented here in this central section or whether you better document it locally (e.g. within the white box template of one building block). Avoid redundant texts."

methods.question: Q15
methods.thinking: The document holds only what stays while the UX and the principles stay, and leaves how each role works inside to where it is built.
steps: Pick one change to how a role works inside, such as its steps, a value it uses or a data's fields, that leaves the UX and the principles as they are.
Read every line, and mark each line the change would make untrue.
Move each marked line to where the role or the data is built, such as its code or its tests, or rewrite it by what stays.
Repeat with a change of another kind, until no line is marked.
grounds: matklad, "ARCHITECTURE.md", matklad.github.io, 2021: "This is the main rule of thumb for ARCHITECTURE — only specify things that are unlikely to frequently change."
matklad, "ARCHITECTURE.md", matklad.github.io, 2021: "Avoid going into details of how each module works, pull this into separate documents or (better) inline documentation."
Ubl, "Design Docs at Google", industrialempathy.com, 2020: "A clear indicator that a doc might not be necessary are design docs that are really implementation manuals."

Fowler, "Software Architecture Guide", martinfowler.com, 2019: "It means that the heart of thinking architecturally about software is to decide what is important, (i.e. what is architectural), and then expend energy on keeping those architectural elements in good condition."
